paper.title: Stochastic Linear Optimization under Bandit Feedback

settings.name_in_paper: Stochastic linear optimization under bandit feedback (compact decision set D in R^n)
unmapped: Costs in [-1,1] with conditional expectation mu.x given history: noise is a bounded martingale difference sequence, not necessarily i.i.d.
Learner is given a barycentric spanner of D; in spanner coordinates D is a subset of [-1,1]^n
settings.definition_quote: Let D ⊂ R^n be a compact (but otherwise arbitrary) set of decisions... Each such choice results in a cost ℓ_t = c_t(x_t) ∈ [−1, 1]. We assume that, regardless of the history H_t, the conditional expectation of c_t is a fixed linear function, i.e., for all x ∈ D, E(c_t(x) | H_t) = µ · x ∈ [−1, 1]. ... R_T = sum_t (µ†x_t − µ†x*)

settings.name_in_paper: Lower bound instance: product of n/2 circles, ±1 costs, mu uniform on D_n/n (lower bound)
unmapped: Decision set D_n = (S^1)^{n/2}, Cartesian product of n/2 unit circles; n even
settings.definition_quote: Let D_n = (S^1)^{n/2} be the Cartesian product of n/2 circles... Our cost functions take values in {−1, +1}, and for every x ∈ D_n, the expected cost is µ · x, where nµ ∈ D_n.

conditions: gap Delta > 0 (Dani et al. gap over extremal points)
tuning: confidence parameter delta given to the algorithm

source.quote: Theorem 1 (Problem Dependent Upper Bound) ... Suppose the decision set D and the true mean µ have a gap ∆ > 0. We have: • ConfidenceBall2 : For all sufficiently large T , the cumulative regret R_T of ConfidenceBall2(D,δ) is with high probability at most O(n^2/∆ log^3 T ). More precisely, Prob(∀T, R_T ≤ 8nβ_T ln(T)/∆) ≥ 1 − δ

results.notes: n is the dimension d. Holds simultaneously for all T. Polynomial-time when D is small/finite; NP-hard in general for polytopes. Section 7 states it extends to time-varying decision sets.

tuning: implemented so that it only chooses extremal points of D

source.quote: • ConfidenceBall1 : If ConfidenceBall1 is implemented so that it only chooses extremal points x_t ∈ D (which is always possible) then, for all sufficiently large T , the cumulative regret R_T of ConfidenceBall1(D,δ) is with high probability at most O(n^3/∆ log^3 T ). More precisely, Prob(∀T, R_T ≤ 8n^2β_T ln(T)/∆) ≥ 1 − δ

results.notes: Efficient with O(n) calls to a linear optimization oracle over D.

source.quote: Theorem 2 (Problem Independent Upper Bound) ... • ConfidenceBall2 : For all sufficiently large T , the cumulative regret R_T of ConfidenceBall2(D,δ) is with high probability at most O*(n√T) ... More precisely, Prob(∀T, R_T ≤ sqrt(8nTβ_T ln T)) ≥ 1 − δ .

• ConfidenceBall1 : For all sufficiently large T , the cumulative regret R_T of ConfidenceBall1(D,δ) is with high probability at most O*(n^{3/2}√T) ... More precisely, Prob(∀T, R_T ≤ sqrt(8n^2Tβ_T ln T)) ≥ 1 − δ .

results.notes: Efficient given linear optimization oracle over D.

source.quote: Theorem 3 (Lower Bound) If µ is chosen uniformly at random from the set D_n/n, and the cost for each x ∈ D_n is in {−1, +1} with mean µ · x, then, for every algorithm, for every T ≥ 1, E R = E_µ E(R | µ) ≥ (1/10) n √T.

results.notes: Regret averaged over a uniform prior on mu (Bayesian), implying a worst-case lower bound. Instance has Delta=0, so it rules out polylog(T) rates on a fixed problem.

_verify.summary: The extraction is accurate. Both upper-bound theorems, each with two algorithm variants, and the lower bound are recorded with the correct constants, the correct β_T, and the correct mapping of the paper's n to d. The settings, the algorithm registry choices (null, since ConfidenceBall/LinRel is not in the registry) and the cited results agree with the source. I propose no corrections.
